summary: Describes an abbreviated format for a composite media feature set, based on a hash of the feature expression that describes the composite. This gives a compact way to refer to long feature descriptions.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of reading out a very long list of what a device can do, you give a short fingerprint that stands for the whole list.

questions: what is a feature set reference
how is a media feature hash calculated
what is the h. prefix in media features
subtitle: A short hash-based name that stands in for a long description of what a device or program can handle.

tldr.problem: A description of a system's media capabilities (a feature set expression from RFC 2533) can get large, and the same description may be repeated or shared by many devices.
tldr.mechanism: Normalize the expression, take its MD5 hash, write the 128-bit result in base-32 and prefix it with h. to get a feature set reference that can be used inside other expressions.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can create such a name without a central authority, and anyone can check that an expression matches a name without a network lookup. How to find the expression behind a name is left to other specifications.

facts.label: Collision chance
facts.value: Less than 1 in 10^38 for two sets

today: RFC 2938 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2533, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the choice of resolution mechanism to other specifications.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
RFC 2533 describes media feature capabilities as a combination of simple media feature tags. RFC 2938 adds an abbreviated format for a composite media feature set, based on a hash of the feature expression that describes it. Readers are assumed to know how RFC 2533 expressions are interpreted.

The RFC defines a few terms. A feature set expression is a string describing a feature set under the RFC 2533 rules. A feature set reference is a brief construct that refers to a feature set. Dereferencing (also called resolution) means replacing a reference with its expression.
sections.plainLanguage: A feature set is a list of things a machine can do. A reference is a short nickname for the list, and looking up the nickname gives you the list back.

sections.title: Motivation and Goals
sections.content:
The media capabilities of a message handling system can be extensive, so the matching expression can reach a significant size. The RFC identifies a requirement that recurring feature sets be named by a single value that can be combined with other elements of an expression.

The goals are: an abbreviated form for any feature set expression; a meaning that does not depend on how the reference is dereferenced; the ability to check that an expression matches a reference without dereferencing (so with no extra network traffic); and no breakage of existing RFC 2533 processors, which can treat a reference like any other expression part.

Suggested uses include a large sub-expression repeated within one expression, and a capability common to a class of devices, such as one class of fax machine with many feature tags but few distinct feature sets. The RFC does not address the "override" or "default" problem, and it does not say how a recipient discovers the expression behind a reference.
sections.plainLanguage: If a long recipe is used again and again, you give it a short name. The short name has to mean the same recipe everywhere, and you should be able to tell if someone gives you the wrong recipe.

sections.title: The Hashed Reference Format
sections.content:
The core idea is a token based on a hash computed over the referenced expression. A hash lets anyone define a global name space without a central naming authority. New feature set tags can be introduced by any party. Local resolution services may be needed, but they cannot vary the meaning of a tag, and a calling application should reject an incorrect value.

The reference is a special auxiliary predicate name of the form h. followed by one or more base-32 digits, where the digits are 0 to 9 and A to V (upper or lower case). In an expression it appears in parentheses, as in (h.SBB5REAOMHC09CP2GM4V07PQP0).

Meaning is by substitution: the referenced expression replaces the reference, and the result is read as a normal expression. If a tag is constrained by both, the RFC 2533 rules apply without regard to origin. The RFC's example combines pix-x=100 and pix-y<=300 with a reference that resolves to pix-x<=200 and pix-y<=150, giving pix-x=100 and pix-y<=150.
sections.plainLanguage: The nickname is made from a fingerprint of the list, so nobody has to hand out nicknames. If two people write the same list, they get the same nickname.

sections.title: Calculating the Hash
sections.content:
The hash is MD5 over the text of the expression after normalization. The expression must fit the filter syntax of RFC 2533. There are three steps.

  1. Whitespace normalization: remove all spaces, CR, LF, TAB and other layout characters, except inside quoted strings.
  2. Case normalization: change unquoted lower-case letters (US-ASCII 97 to 122) to upper case (65 to 90).
  3. Hash computation: apply MD5 (RFC 1321) to the normalized string as US-ASCII octets. The result is a 128-bit (16 octet) value, which is converted to base-32.

Removing all whitespace can sometimes make an invalid string. The RFC says that is fine, because it is done only to compute the hash. Case normalization is acceptable because feature tag and token matching is case insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Before fingerprinting, you tidy the list the same way every time: squeeze out the spaces and make the letters capitals. Then two lists that only look different still give the same fingerprint.

sections.title: Base-32 Encoding
sections.content:
Each base-32 character stands for 5 successive bits, so each group of 8 characters encodes 5 octets (40 bits). Digits 0 to 9 have values 0 to 9 and letters A to V have values 10 to 31. A leftover group of 1, 2, 3 or 4 octets is encoded by 2, 4, 5 or 7 characters, with spare bits set to zero when encoding and discarded when decoding.

For an MD5 value, the first 15 octets give 24 characters and the final octet gives two, so the hash part has 26 characters.

The RFC explains the choice. Base64 would be shorter (21 rather than 26 characters), but an auxiliary predicate name has the syntax of a feature tag, and feature tag matching is case insensitive. Base36 was considered but would need extended precision multiplication and division to encode and decode.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is written using only digits and capital letters, so it still works when someone changes capitals to small letters.

sections.title: Resolving a Reference
sections.content:
The RFC does not require any one way to dereference a reference. Specific mechanisms are expected to be defined by applications that use them. Whatever the mechanism, hash rules take precedence: an expression may not replace a hash-based reference unless it yields the correct hash.

Two options are sketched. A query protocol such as HTTP or LDAP could provide a resolution service, returning the expression or a full definition, and URN resolution through DNS NAPTR (RFC 2168) might find the server. Alternatively the definition can be given inline in a where clause using auxiliary predicate syntax. It is an error if the inline expression does not yield the hash in the predicate name.

The inline form fits a follow-up in a conversation: one side sends a reference, the other says it does not understand it, and the first side sends it again with the definition attached.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint cannot be turned back into the list by itself. You ask someone, or they attach the list, and you check it against the fingerprint.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows small expressions such as (& (dpi=100) (h.SBB5REAOMHC09CP2GM4V07PQP0) ), where the reference stands for (& (pix-x<=200) (pix-y<=150) ). It also shows a larger alternative of four fax capability sets reduced to one reference.

The fax examples come from Internet fax work. A "simple mode" system, described by a long expression with TIFF-minimal, color=Binary and image-coding=MH, is expressed by one hash reference. A full-color fax system shares JPEG-related capabilities between its grey and full-color branches, and pulling those out into a single reference shortens the expression.
sections.plainLanguage: A fax machine with a long list of abilities can say its nickname instead, or give the shared parts a nickname so it only writes them once.

sections.title: Security, Internationalization and Collisions
sections.content:
Security considerations are mostly those of capability identification in general. One added concern is that a specific feature set identifier may reveal more about a system than the current transaction needs.

On internationalization, feature set expressions and URI strings are currently US-ASCII only, so the spec is not affected. If later syntax allows other characters, a canonical form for hashing would be needed, such as UTF-8, and case conversion would need proper definition.

Appendix A is commentary on hash collisions. Assuming MD5's 128-bit output is spread evenly over 2^128 values, the chance that two distinct expressions share a hash is less than 1 in 10^38. The "birthday paradox" makes the chance grow with the number of feature sets: the table gives about 1E-15 for 1E12 sets and about 1E-3 for 1E18. If expressions are made by hand, the RFC concludes the risk of a wrong match is negligible compared with other failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different lists could in theory get the same fingerprint, but it is so unlikely that it is not worth worrying about for lists people write by hand.
